game.eq.name: Guess the Band
game.eq.instructions: Listen, then drag along the scale to where you think the boost or cut is. You don't have to be exact - land inside the tolerance band and it counts.
game.compression.name: Guess the Compression
game.compression.instructions: Listen to the drum hits, then guess how strong the compression is. Judge it by how much the loud hits get pulled down relative to the quiet ones, not just by overall loudness.
game.reverb.name: Guess the Reverb
game.reverb.instructions: Listen to the repeating hit, then guess the reverb type. Room and Hall differ mainly in decay length, Plate is a bright studio character with no real geometry, and Spring has a distinctive metallic clang.
game.pan.name: Guess the Pan Position
game.pan.instructions: Listen, then guess where the sound is panned. Equal-power panning keeps loudness constant across positions, so trust your sense of direction rather than loudness.
game.delay.name: Guess the Delay Time
game.delay.instructions: Listen to the echo, then guess the delay time. Very short delay times blur into the source instead of sounding like a distinct echo - the same effect behind widening and chorus tricks.
game.distortion.name: Guess the Distortion
game.distortion.instructions: Listen, then guess the type of distortion. Soft and hard clipping generate different harmonics - even-order ones read as warmer, odd-order as harsher and more aggressive.
game.stereowidth.name: Guess the Stereo Width
game.stereowidth.instructions: Listen, then guess how wide the stereo image is. Width comes from decorrelation between channels, not just panning - always worth checking a wide mix still holds together in mono.
game.db.name: Guess the Gain Change
game.db.instructions: Listen, then guess how much the level changed. Differences below roughly 1 dB get hard to reliably tell apart, so don't expect every step to feel equally obvious.
game.frequencyrange.name: Name the Range
game.frequencyrange.instructions: Listen, then click the frequency range you think was boosted or cut. Treat the named ranges as a starting map for where a problem tends to live, not a fixed rule.
game.eq.benefit: Learn to hear which octave band a boost or cut lands in - the core skill behind every EQ move you'll ever make.
game.compression.benefit: Train your ear for how hard a compressor is squeezing, so you can set a ratio by ear instead of by number.
game.reverb.benefit: Tell a room from a hall from a plate from a spring - the difference between choosing a reverb and guessing at one.
game.pan.benefit: Sharpen your sense of where a sound sits across the stereo field, the foundation of a wide, uncluttered mix.
game.delay.benefit: Learn to judge delay time by ear, so you can match an echo to a track's tempo and mood without a calculator.
game.distortion.benefit: Recognise the character each kind of saturation adds, and pick the one that flatters the source.
game.stereowidth.benefit: Hear how wide a source really is - the skill that keeps a mix big without collapsing in mono.
game.db.benefit: Calibrate your ear to level changes in dB, so your fader moves become deliberate instead of exploratory.
game.frequencyrange.benefit: Learn the named ranges - sub-bass through air - so you can describe a problem before you reach for a knob.

choice.narrow: Almost mono. The sides are pulled in, so everything sits near the centre.
choice.normal: The stereo image as recorded. Nothing added, nothing taken away.
choice.wide: The sides are lifted. The edges pull outward and the centre feels less crowded.

ui.soundsPickCategory: Pick a category on the left to see its clips, then click one to train on that clip alone.
choice.room: A small hard space. The tail is short and you can still hear the first few reflections separately.
choice.chamber: Bigger than a room, smaller than a hall. Dense from the start, with no obvious early reflections.
choice.hall: A long, thick tail. Individual reflections have merged; what is left is one slowly fading cloud.
choice.plate: Bright and immediate, with no sense of a real geometry. A sheet of metal, not a room.
choice.spring: A metallic clang with an audible boing. The mechanism is a coil, and you can hear that it is one.
choice.softclipping: The peaks round off gradually. Warmer, thicker, still recognisably the same sound.
choice.hardclipping: The peaks are cut flat. Harsh and buzzy, with harmonics that were not in the source at all.
choice.tapesaturation: Soft compression plus a rolled-off top. Thicker in the middle and darker at the edges.
choice.overdrive: Asymmetric clipping, so it adds even harmonics. Fuller and more vocal than a symmetric clip.
choice.extrawide: The sides are pushed well past natural. Impressive on its own, thin in mono.
choice.subbass: 20-60 Hz. Felt more than heard - the part that moves air rather than the part with pitch.
choice.bass: 60-250 Hz. Weight and body. Too much here is what makes a mix sound thick.
choice.lowmids: 250-500 Hz. Warmth, and the first place mud collects when too many things overlap.
choice.mids: 500 Hz - 2 kHz. Where most instruments live, and where boxiness and honk sit.
choice.highmids: 2-4 kHz. Attack and intelligibility. The ear is most sensitive here, so a little goes far.
choice.presence: 4-6 kHz. Definition and edge - and where sibilance starts to become a problem.
choice.air: 6-20 kHz. Openness and sheen. Too much turns into hiss rather than into brightness.

guide.comp.attack:
How fast compression kicks in after a peak crosses the threshold. A fast attack (0.1-5 ms) catches transients and controls them; a slower attack (20-30 ms) lets the initial hit through before clamping down - the classic way to keep drums punchy while still taming the sustain. A good habit is starting slow and only speeding up as much as actually needed, since an extremely fast attack can visibly distort a low-frequency waveform.
Learn more: Bobby Owsinski - The Mixing Engineer's Handbook.
guide.comp.dryWet:
Blends compressed (wet) with uncompressed (dry) signal. Parallel compression - wet below 100% - adds density and sustain from the compressed signal while keeping the dry signal's original transients and dynamics intact. Push the wet amount too far and fast material can turn to mush - a modest blend usually keeps most of the benefit.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.comp.knee:
How gradually compression ramps in around the threshold. 0 dB is a hard knee - compression switches on suddenly right at the threshold; higher values ease in gradually before and after it, which usually sounds smoother and less noticeable on program material - though a very wide knee starts shaping the signal noticeably below the displayed threshold number.
Learn more: Bobby Owsinski - The Mixing Engineer's Handbook.
guide.comp.makeup:
Restores loudness lost to compression - it doesn't change the dynamics, only the overall level afterward. Raise it to bring a compressed signal back up to match (or exceed) the original's perceived loudness. Comparing compressed and dry signal at mismatched volumes is one of the easiest ways to fool yourself about whether the compression itself is actually doing anything useful.
Learn more: Bob Katz - Mastering Audio: The Art and the Science.
guide.comp.ratio:
How much compression is applied above the threshold. 4:1 means 4 dB over the threshold becomes 1 dB at the output. 2-4:1 reads as gentle leveling; 8:1 and up starts to feel like limiting - though a high ratio alone won't sound obviously hard without a threshold set to match it.
Learn more: Bobby Owsinski - The Mixing Engineer's Handbook.
guide.comp.release:
How fast compression lets go after the signal drops back below threshold. Too short on fast material can cause audible pumping (gain visibly breathing with the rhythm); too long can feel sluggish, not recovering before the next peak arrives. Watching the gain-reduction meter's movement over time, not just its peak value, is the more reliable way to judge whether release is actually right.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.comp.threshold:
The level above which the compressor starts working. -12 dB means only peaks louder than -12 dB get turned down; everything quieter passes through untouched. Lower thresholds mean more of the signal gets compressed - worth choosing together with ratio and knee rather than dialing each in isolation.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.eq.freq.0:
Sub/bass fundamentals - weight and body. Boosting here adds low-end power; too much turns into boominess or mud on smaller speakers. A high-pass just above this zone is often more useful than a boost - judge it by ear in context, not from one fixed cutoff number.
Learn more: Mike Senior - Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio.
guide.eq.freq.1:
Low mids - warmth and fullness, but also where several instruments stacked together turn muddy or boxy. Cutting here is often more useful than boosting; if a real boost is unavoidable, splitting it between this frequency and its octave above can sound less resonant than one big narrow bump.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.eq.freq.2:
Mids - the body and fullness of most instruments and vocals lives here. Small moves go a long way: this is the range where the ear notices a boost fastest, sometimes from as little as 2-3 dB.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.eq.freq.3:
Presence - clarity and forwardness, close to the vocal formant range the ear is most sensitive to (and to the ear canal's own resonance around 2.6-3.5 kHz). Useful for intelligibility, but a fixed deep cut here can strip speech of clarity - a gentler, dynamic touch is safer.
Learn more: F. Alton Everest - Master Handbook of Acoustics.
guide.eq.freq.4:
Upper presence - definition and bite, the edge that helps a source cut through a busy mix without turning the level up. A narrow bell aimed right at the bite reads differently than a broad shelf lifting the whole region - pick the shape for the actual job, not just the frequency.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.eq.freq.5:
Brilliance - air and sparkle, but also where sibilance ('s'/'t' hiss on vocals) and cymbal harshness live - boost carefully. If sibilance is the actual problem, a dedicated de-esser targeting just this band usually beats pulling the whole zone down with static EQ.
Learn more: Mike Senior - Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio.
guide.eq.freq.6:
Air - a sense of openness and space; there's no fundamental content up here, just harmonics, so it's easy to overdo without realizing it. Even a boost this high can raise the true peak more than expected - worth rechecking levels after a generous lift.
Learn more: Mike Senior - Mixing Secrets for the Small Studio.
guide.verb.damping:
How quickly high frequencies die out in the tail. More damping sounds darker and more absorbent, like a room full of soft furnishings; less damping sounds brighter and more metallic, like a hard-surfaced space. Too little damping on a long decay can leave a bright, harsh tail hanging around far longer than the low end needs to.
Learn more: F. Alton Everest - Master Handbook of Acoustics.
guide.verb.decay:
RT60: the time, in seconds, the tail takes to fall by 60 dB. Longer decay sounds like a bigger, more reflective space; 1.5-2.5 s is typical for vocal ambience, while shorter times (0.3-0.8 s) keep a dense mix from getting washed out. In a real space the high end usually dies out faster than the low end - Damping below models that independently of this overall decay time.
Learn more: F. Alton Everest - Master Handbook of Acoustics.
guide.verb.dryWet:
Blends the reverberated (wet) signal with the untreated (dry) source. Lower wet amounts keep the source upfront with just a hint of space; higher amounts push it further back. When a reverb is shared across several tracks via a send, the common convention is to run the return itself near 100% wet and do the dry/wet blending per-track instead, right here.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
guide.verb.preDelay:
The gap between the dry sound and when the reverb starts. 20-50 ms keeps a vocal's consonants clear before the space blooms in - without it, the tail can swallow the start of the sound. It's often tuned together with Size and Decay as one bigger, longer, later-starting space, rather than moved on its own.
Learn more: Philip Newell - Recording Studio Design.
guide.verb.size:
How far apart the reflecting surfaces are: it spaces the early reflections and thins the tail, without changing how long it lasts. On Plate it is the size of the sheet, on Spring the length of the coil - a longer spring repeats later and drips more slowly. Pushed too far on a room it can blur a transient's attack into the reflections.
Learn more: F. Alton Everest - Master Handbook of Acoustics.
guide.verb.type:
The reverb algorithm: Room and Hall are size-based spaces (Room short and dense, Hall long with a smooth, spacious decay), Plate is a bright, smooth studio character with no real-room geometry, Spring is the metallic, clanging character of a guitar-amp spring tank. Reusing the same type/settings across several tracks (rather than a unique reverb per source) often reads as a more cohesive shared space in a full mix.
Learn more: F. Alton Everest - Master Handbook of Acoustics.
guide.verb.width:
How wide the reverb's stereo image is, independent of the dry signal's width - a narrower tail keeps the space subtle and centered, a wider one surrounds the source. Controlling width here directly is generally safer than panning the wet return itself, which can introduce its own left/right phase issues - always worth a quick mono check either way.
Learn more: Roey Izhaki - Mixing Audio.
mod.comp.attack.name: Attack
mod.comp.attack.step1: 1 ms. The compressor catches the very front of every hit, so the crack of the snare is gone - it is being squashed before you hear it.
mod.comp.attack.step2: 20 ms. Now the front of each hit gets through untouched and only what follows it is held down. This is what people mean by a compressor adding punch: it is not adding anything, it is turning down everything except the punch.
mod.comp.attack.step3: 80 ms. So slow that most of each hit is over before it reacts. On fast material this is close to doing nothing.
mod.comp.attack.try: Find the attack where the snare still cracks but the tail after it is controlled. Too fast and it flattens the hit; too slow and it misses the hit entirely.
mod.comp.attack.why: How long the compressor waits before clamping down on a transient.
mod.comp.dryWet.name: Parallel compression
mod.comp.dryWet.step1: 100% wet with heavy compression. Everything is level and nothing has any dynamics left.
mod.comp.dryWet.step2: 40% wet. The squashed version lifts the quiet parts while the dry version keeps the transients intact. You get the loudness of the first without losing the shape of the second.
mod.comp.dryWet.try: Find the blend where the quiet detail comes up but the hits still have their shape. This is how you get density without flattening.
mod.comp.dryWet.why: Blends the compressed signal back in with the untouched one.
mod.comp.knee.name: Knee
mod.comp.knee.step1: Hard knee, 0 dB. Below the threshold nothing, above it the full ratio. The transition has an edge you can hear.
mod.comp.knee.step2: 12 dB. The ratio now eases in over a 12 dB span around the threshold, so quiet material gets a little compression and loud material gets all of it. Same threshold, softer arrival.
mod.comp.knee.try: Widen the knee until the compressor stops announcing itself. You are listening for the moment gain reduction starts to become hard to point at.
mod.comp.knee.why: How abruptly compression arrives as the signal crosses the threshold.
mod.comp.makeup.name: Makeup gain
mod.comp.makeup.step1: 6 dB of gain reduction and no makeup. The compressed version is quieter, so of course it sounds worse - you have not heard compression yet, you have heard a level drop.
mod.comp.makeup.step2: Makeup up by about what the meter is taking off. Now the two are the same loudness, and the difference you hear is the actual difference.
mod.comp.makeup.try: Match the compressed sound to the bypassed one. Louder always sounds better, and matching level is the only way to hear what the compressor actually did.
mod.comp.makeup.why: Puts back the level the compression took away.
mod.comp.ratio.name: Ratio
mod.comp.ratio.step1: Threshold set, ratio at 1:1. Over the line, nothing happens - one decibel in, one decibel out.
mod.comp.ratio.step2: 3:1. Three decibels over the threshold come out as one. The hits are still hits, just less far apart.
mod.comp.ratio.step3: 12:1. Practically a wall - the signal barely gets above the threshold at all any more. Listen for what it costs: the drums stop breathing.
mod.comp.ratio.try: Set the ratio so the drums are evened out but still hit. Somewhere around 4:1 is a normal working answer; 20:1 is a different job.
mod.comp.ratio.why: How hard it pushes back once the signal is over the threshold.
mod.comp.release.name: Release
mod.comp.release.step1: 30 ms. It lets go almost immediately after each hit, so the level jumps back up between them. That is the pumping people either love or fix.
mod.comp.release.step2: 150 ms. It recovers in the gaps but not inside them. This is the ordinary working answer for a groove at this tempo.
mod.comp.release.step3: 700 ms. It never gets back up before the next hit arrives, so the gain reduction just sits there. The compressor has stopped responding to the music and become a volume knob.
mod.comp.release.try: Set the release so the compressor recovers between hits rather than pumping across them. The gain reduction meter should return to zero and then move again, not hover.
mod.comp.release.why: How long it takes to let go once the signal drops back down.
mod.comp.threshold.name: Threshold
mod.comp.threshold.step1: Threshold all the way up. The compressor is doing nothing - everything is below it, so nothing is above it.
mod.comp.threshold.step2: At -12 dB only the peaks poke above the line, so only the peaks get touched. The rest of the sound is untouched.
mod.comp.threshold.step3: At -30 dB almost everything is above the line. The whole signal is being held down now, not just its loudest moments - which is a different effect, not more of the same one.
mod.comp.threshold.try: Bring the threshold down until the loud parts of the bass are held back but the quiet parts are still untouched. Watch the gain reduction meter: you want it moving, not pinned.
mod.comp.threshold.why: The level above which the compressor starts working at all.
mod.comp.walk.attack.name: Attack: why fast kills the punch
mod.comp.walk.attack.step1: Compressor out of the way: ratio 1:1, so nothing is happening. Listen to the front of each hit - that first few milliseconds is the transient, and it is most of what makes a drum sound like a drum rather than like a tone.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step2: Now 4:1 at -18 dB with a 1 ms attack. The compressor catches the transient itself, so the loudest part of every hit is the part that gets flattened. Watch the meter: it slams down on each hit. The result is even - and blunt.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step3: Same settings, attack 30 ms. Now the transient gets through before the gain reduction arrives, and only the body behind it is compressed. Louder attack against quieter body reads as *more* punch - from a compressor, which is supposed to reduce dynamics.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step4: That is the counterintuitive part worth keeping: a slow attack makes things hit harder, a fast attack makes them sit still. Neither is correct - they answer different questions. "Control the level" wants fast; "make it punch" wants slow.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step5: Attack is relative to the source, not an absolute. 30 ms on a snare lets the crack through; 30 ms on a sustained pad is instant, because a pad has no transient to miss. This is why a preset that worked on drums does nothing recognisable on a synth - the number moved into a different envelope.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step6: One caution before you go fast: at very short attack times a compressor starts tracking individual *cycles* of low frequency rather than the envelope over them, and that is distortion, not level control. On bass it is audible as a growl that was not there before.
mod.comp.walk.attack.step7: Back to something usable: 4:1, 20 ms, and compare against bypass. The question is never "is it compressed" - it is whether the thing you wanted to hear got louder relative to the thing you did not.
mod.comp.walk.attack.why: Why a slow attack punches harder.
mod.comp.walk.glue.name: Bus Glue Compression
mod.comp.walk.glue.step2: A gentle 2:1 ratio with a high threshold - just brushing the loudest peaks, not squashing everything.
mod.comp.walk.glue.step3: A slow 30 ms attack lets transients through untouched - the classic glue-compression setting.
mod.comp.walk.glue.step4: A soft knee blends the compression in gradually instead of switching on abruptly at the threshold.
mod.comp.walk.glue.step5: The goal here is only a couple of dB of gain reduction, not ten - watch the meter rather than chasing a bigger number.
mod.comp.walk.glue.step6: Makeup Gain +2 dB brings the level back without overdoing it.
mod.comp.walk.glue.why: Two or three dB that hold a mix together.
mod.comp.walk.release.name: Release, and where pumping comes from
mod.comp.walk.release.step1: 4:1 at -18 dB, attack 20 ms, release very long - 800 ms. The compressor grabs and then holds on. Between hits it has still not let go, so quiet passages stay quiet and the track loses its own shape.
mod.comp.walk.release.step2: Now 30 ms. It releases fully between every hit, which means the gain is moving constantly - up in the gaps, down on the hits. That audible breathing in and out is pumping. On a drum bus it can be the effect you want; under a vocal it is a distraction that never resolves.
mod.comp.walk.release.step3: Very fast release has the same problem fast attack does, from the other end: below roughly one cycle of the lowest frequency present, the envelope follows the waveform instead of the loudness, and you get harmonic distortion. Low frequencies are long - 50 Hz is 20 ms per cycle - which is why bass needs slower release than a hi-hat does.
mod.comp.walk.release.step4: A useful starting point: let it recover roughly in time with the music. Around 150 ms sits near an eighth note at 100 BPM, so the gain moves with the groove rather than against it. Then adjust by ear - the tempo is a starting place, not a rule.
mod.comp.walk.release.step5: The last honest thing about both knobs: aim for a few dB of gain reduction and judge the result by bypassing, not by the meter. A meter shows how hard the compressor is working, which is not the same question as whether the track got better.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.name: Vocal Compression
mod.comp.walk.vocal.step2: Set threshold to -18 dB - the compressor kicks in on louder peaks.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.step4: Attack 8 ms - quick enough to catch the loud syllables, slow enough that the consonant at the front of each word keeps its edge.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.step5: Release 150 ms - a smooth recovery back to unity gain.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.step6: Add a 6 dB knee - the same ratio now eases in gradually around the threshold instead of switching on abruptly.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.step7: Makeup Gain +4 dB - restore the loudness the compressor took away.
mod.comp.walk.vocal.why: A vocal chain, knob by knob.
mod.eq.frequency.name: Frequency
mod.eq.frequency.step1: A +9 dB bell at 250 Hz. Warm, thick - it is in the body of the sound.
mod.eq.frequency.step2: The same bell at 1 kHz. Nasal, honky - this is the mids most boosts end up in by accident.
mod.eq.frequency.step3: And at 5 kHz. Edge, presence, and the start of harshness.
mod.eq.frequency.try: Sweep the frequency knob until the boost you hear sits where you think it should, then listen to it move above and below.
mod.eq.frequency.why: Where a boost is. The one EQ skill everything else rests on.
mod.eq.gain.name: Gain
mod.eq.gain.step1: A bell at 800 Hz, +6 dB. Obvious.
mod.eq.gain.step2: +2 dB. Still there, if you switch back and forth - this is the size of most real moves.
mod.eq.gain.step3: -6 dB. A cut takes something away rather than adding a colour; it is often heard as the sound getting clearer, not quieter.
mod.eq.gain.try: Set the gain until the change is as big as you want it, then halve it and listen again. Most useful moves are smaller than they first seem.
mod.eq.gain.why: How much - and which way. A 3 dB cut and a 3 dB boost are different sounds.
mod.eq.highpass.name: High-pass
mod.eq.highpass.step1: A high-pass at 30 Hz: nothing audible is gone, only rumble.
mod.eq.highpass.step2: At 120 Hz. The note is still there, its weight is not.
mod.eq.highpass.step3: At 300 Hz. Thin - this is a telephone, not a bass.
mod.eq.highpass.try: Raise the cutoff until the bass note starts to lose its weight, then back it off until it comes back. That is the edge.
mod.eq.highpass.why: Where the bottom stops. The most used filter in a mix, and the most overdone.
mod.eq.q.name: Width (Q)
mod.eq.q.step1: A wide bell, Q 0.5, +8 dB at 1 kHz. It colours everything around it - a tilt more than a spot.
mod.eq.q.step2: Q 8. The same boost, now a single ringing pitch.
mod.eq.q.try: Narrow the band until it stops sounding like a tone change and starts sounding like one ringing note. That point is higher than you think.
mod.eq.q.why: How much of the spectrum a band takes with it.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.name: High-pass: what it costs
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step1: Flat, one band, doing nothing. Listen to the low end as it is - you need the before, or the after means nothing.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step2: A gentle high-pass at 40 Hz, Q 0.7. Below this sits rumble, handle noise and room energy that costs headroom and gives nothing back. On most sources this is the safest EQ move there is - and on a kick or a bass it is already too high.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step3: Now drag it up to 150 Hz. Somewhere on the way, the source stops sounding cleaner and starts sounding thin. That point is not a number you can be told - it moves with the instrument, the arrangement and the speaker you are on.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step4: Q 4 at the same frequency. The curve now lifts just above the cutoff before it falls. That bump is real: a resonant pole pair peaks near its corner, and a high-Q high-pass adds energy exactly where you were trying to remove it. It can be useful - it is also why a 'tighter' filter can make a bass boomier.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step5: Back to Q 0.7, and one more pass filter stacked on top: two in series is a steeper slope. Steeper removes more, faster - and every pole you add turns the phase further near the corner. A minimum-phase filter cannot change amplitude without changing phase; the two are the same fact seen twice.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step6: Why that matters: phase rotation is inaudible on a solo'd track and very audible when two tracks are summed. High-pass a kick and a bass at the same corner with steep filters and the region just above it can partially cancel - the fault is not in either track, it is in the sum. Bypass and compare on the mix, not on the source.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step7: This is why 'brickwall' is a description, not a goal. An extremely steep filter needs many poles, and pays for them in phase smear and pre-ringing around the corner. If a gentle slope gets you there, it is the better filter - reach for steep when the problem is genuinely narrow and genuinely in the way.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.step8: Left where it started: one gentle high-pass at 40 Hz. Bypass to check that it is still an improvement - the move most worth making is the one you can still hear the point of.
mod.eq.walk.highpass.why: What a high-pass takes with it.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.name: Low-pass and the top end
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.step1: Flat again. Listen to the top: cymbals, breath, the noise floor of whatever this was recorded on.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.step2: A low-pass at 16 kHz. Almost nothing is missing - but hiss, cymbal wash and converter noise from several tracks add up, and removing what an instrument never produced costs it nothing.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.step3: Down to 6 kHz. Now it is an effect rather than housekeeping - the sound moves backwards and gets darker. That is the same cue distance gives you in a real room: air absorbs high frequencies over distance, so dull reads as far away.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.step4: A high shelf can do a gentler version of the same thing. Set -4 dB from 6 kHz up: the top is quieter but still there, which is usually what you meant when you reached for the low-pass.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.step5: Both are correct tools. The pass filter says 'nothing above here'; the shelf says 'less above here'. Reaching for the first when you meant the second is how a mix ends up dull instead of clean.
mod.eq.walk.lowpass.why: Where the top end stops being useful.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.name: Find & Fix a Resonance
mod.eq.walk.resonance.step1: Flat, one band ready to hunt with.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.step2: Search: a narrow bell, Q 8, boosted +8 dB, at 400 Hz. Sweeping a boost like this through a source makes whatever rings or honks jump out - the boost exaggerates the problem so you can find it.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.step3: Found it. Flip the same band into a cut, -4 dB. The search boost is never the fix; it only showed you where to look.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.step4: Now widen it to Q 1.5. A cut as narrow as the search sounds surgical and phasey; a slightly wider one sits in the sound.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.step5: Compare: step back to hear the search boost again, or finish.
mod.eq.walk.resonance.why: Boost to find it, cut to fix it.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.name: Vocal EQ Basics
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step1: The untreated sound. One band, flat - nothing is being done yet.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step2: Low-end warmth: a low shelf at 120 Hz, +1.5 dB. A shelf lifts everything below its corner, not one spot - which is why it reads as weight rather than as a tone.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step3: Presence: a bell at 3 kHz, +3 dB. This is where consonants and the edge of the voice live; a little brings the words forward.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step4: Mud: a bell at 250 Hz, -3 dB. Most boxy, cardboard-sounding vocals have too much here, and cutting it lets the presence boost do less.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step5: Air: a high shelf at 10 kHz, +2 dB. Openness above the voice itself - too much and it turns into hiss rather than brightness.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.step6: Compare: step back to hear it without, or finish to put the plugin back the way it was.
mod.eq.walk.vocal.why: Four moves on a voice, one at a time.
mod.verb.damping.name: Damping
mod.verb.damping.step1: Damping at zero. The tail stays as bright at the end as it was at the start, which no real space does.
mod.verb.damping.step2: 80%. The same decay time, but the top end is gone long before the bottom is. That is what soft surfaces do to a room, and it is most of what makes a reverb sit behind a mix instead of on top of it.
mod.verb.damping.try: Raise the damping until the tail goes dark without getting shorter. Every real room does this; a reverb that does not is the thing that sounds fake.
mod.verb.damping.why: How much faster the high frequencies die than the low ones.
mod.verb.decay.name: Decay
mod.verb.decay.step1: 0.6 seconds. The tail is gone before you have finished noticing it - this is ambience, not reverb you can point at.
mod.verb.decay.step2: 2.5 seconds. Now it is an effect you would describe. Notice you have not made it louder, only longer.
mod.verb.decay.step3: 7 seconds. Long enough that the space becomes the subject and whatever went into it stops being legible.
mod.verb.decay.try: Set a decay that fits the gap between hits. If the tail is still going when the next hit lands, the two are fighting.
mod.verb.decay.why: How long the tail takes to fade to nothing.
mod.verb.dryWet.name: Mix
mod.verb.dryWet.step1: Fully dry. Whatever is set above this makes no difference at all yet - the mix control is the one that decides whether any of the others matter.
mod.verb.dryWet.step2: 25%. Enough to place the sound somewhere, not enough to notice as an effect. This is where most mix reverb lives.
mod.verb.dryWet.step3: 75%. Now the space is louder than the thing in it.
mod.verb.dryWet.try: Bring the mix up until you can just hear the space, then back it off slightly. Almost every reverb that sounds wrong is a good reverb with too much of it.
mod.verb.dryWet.why: How much of the wet signal is in the output at all.
mod.verb.preDelay.name: Pre-delay
mod.verb.preDelay.step1: 0 ms. The reverb starts at the same instant as the hit, so the two are one event and the hit loses its edge.
mod.verb.preDelay.step2: 40 ms. The hit lands first, alone, and the space arrives just after it. Same reverb, same amount of it, and the source is suddenly in front instead of inside.
mod.verb.preDelay.step3: 140 ms. Far enough that it stops reading as a room and starts reading as a separate echo. Useful, but it is a different effect now.
mod.verb.preDelay.try: Raise the pre-delay until the hit separates from its own tail. This is how you get a big space without losing the front of the sound.
mod.verb.preDelay.why: The silence between the dry sound and the first of its reflections.
mod.verb.size.name: Size
mod.verb.size.step1: Small. Reflections arrive close together, so the tail is dense and slightly boxy.
mod.verb.size.step2: Large, and the decay has not moved. The reflections are now spread out - the same length of tail with far less packed into it.
mod.verb.size.try: Change size without touching decay. You are listening for how *dense* the tail is, not how long - a small room with a long decay is a real and quite strange sound.
mod.verb.size.why: How far apart the reflecting surfaces are.
mod.verb.type.name: Type
mod.verb.type.step1: Room. Short, dense, early reflections close together - it sounds like the sound happened somewhere rather than nowhere.
mod.verb.type.step2: Hall. The same hit in something much bigger: the reflections arrive later and take far longer to die away.
mod.verb.type.step3: Plate. Not a room at all - a sheet of metal. Very dense from the first instant, with no sense of a wall anywhere.
mod.verb.type.step4: Spring. A metal coil, and it announces itself: that boing is the sound bouncing along the spring and back.
mod.verb.type.try: Listen to the same hit through each of the four and find the one you would call metallic. Type is the one reverb decision you make with your ears before you touch a number.
mod.verb.type.why: Which kind of space or device the tail is pretending to be.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.name: Three ways to say bigger
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step1: A small, dry-ish room to start from. Decay, Size and Damping all make a space sound larger or smaller, and they are not interchangeable - this walks what each one actually changes.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step2: Decay to 3.5 s, nothing else touched. The room did not get bigger - it got *more reflective*. This is the difference between a hall and a tiled bathroom: how long energy survives, not how far it travels.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step3: Decay back down, Size up instead. Now the early reflections arrive further apart, which is the cue that actually says "large room". A short decay in a big space is a real thing - a well-treated concert hall behaves like that.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step4: Damping is the third one, and it is the most physical. Real surfaces absorb high frequencies faster than low ones, so a real tail gets darker as it decays. At damping 0 the tail keeps its top end all the way out, which no room does - it reads as metallic and artificial.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step5: Damping up to 75%. Same decay time, but the high end dies away first, and the space suddenly has surfaces in it - curtains, wood, people. This is usually the knob that makes a reverb stop sounding like a plugin.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.step6: The last one is not on this plugin, and is worth saying anyway: reverb belongs on a send, not on every insert. One room that several tracks share sounds like a place; a different room per track sounds like several recordings edited together - and costs several times the CPU to get there.
mod.verb.walk.bigger.why: Decay, size and damping are not the same knob.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.name: Pre-delay: staying in front of the room
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step1: Completely dry. This is the reference - a source with no space around it at all, which is also what a close microphone in a treated room gives you.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step2: A hall at 30% wet, pre-delay 0. The reverb starts at the same instant the sound does, so the two are glued together. It sounds distant, and the words get harder to follow - the tail is covering the very consonants that make them legible.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step3: Same reverb, pre-delay 40 ms. The dry sound now arrives alone and the room follows it. Nothing about the tail changed - only when it starts - and the source has moved forward, stayed intelligible, and kept its space.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step4: Why that works: the ear locates a sound by what reaches it *first*, and for a few tens of milliseconds afterwards it treats reflections as part of the same event rather than as a second one. Pre-delay puts the room inside that window, so you hear one sound in a space rather than two sounds.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step5: There is a limit. Push it to 120 ms and the reflection stops being part of the sound and becomes an echo - a separate event, arriving late. Somewhere between those two it stops being space and starts being rhythm.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.step6: A practical trick: pre-delay in time with the track keeps the room from smearing across the grid. Back to 40 ms - and note that on a fast, dense arrangement, less wet with more pre-delay usually beats more wet with none.
mod.verb.walk.predelay.why: Keeping the source in front of its room.
mod.verb.walk.tail.name: Bright vs. Dark Tail
mod.verb.walk.tail.step2: Add a Hall reverb with low damping - the tail stays bright and metallic all the way through its decay.
mod.verb.walk.tail.step3: Now raise damping a lot, same decay time - the top end dies out much faster than the low end.
mod.verb.walk.tail.step4: In a real room, high frequencies almost always fade faster than low ones - damping is what lets a reverb imitate that independently of the overall decay length.
mod.verb.walk.tail.step5: Compare: step back to hear the bright tail again, or close the lesson to keep the darker one.
mod.verb.walk.tail.why: Why real rooms get darker as they fade.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.name: Space for Vocals
mod.verb.walk.vocal.step2: Add Plate reverb: 1.5 s decay, 20% wet.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.step3: Pre-Delay 40 ms - separate the voice from the reverb before it blooms.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.step4: Increase damping - remove brightness from the tail.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.step5: Narrow the stereo width a touch - the reverb hugs the center instead of surrounding the voice.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.step6: Compare with Hall at 2.5 s decay - a different kind of space entirely.
mod.verb.walk.vocal.why: A plate for a voice, then a hall to compare.
mod.verb.width.name: Width
mod.verb.width.step1: Full width. The tail occupies the whole image while the source stays where it was.
mod.verb.width.step2: 30%. The tail collapses toward the middle and sits on top of the source instead of around it - the same amount of reverb, much more in the way.
mod.verb.width.try: Narrow the tail and listen to what happens to the dry sound's position. A wide reverb on a centred source is the oldest trick there is for making something feel bigger without moving it.
mod.verb.width.why: How far across the image the tail is spread.
preset.comp.0.name: Vocal Smoothing
preset.comp.0.what: Moderate ratio with a soft knee and a fast-but-not-instant attack: it evens out a performance without flattening the consonants that carry the words.
preset.comp.1.name: Punchy Drums
preset.comp.1.what: A slow 20 ms attack deliberately lets the stick hit through before the compressor closes, so the transient stays sharp and only the body behind it is controlled.
preset.comp.2.name: Bass Control
preset.comp.2.what: Low threshold and a long release, so the gain settles rather than moving with each note - a fast release on bass audibly pumps in time with the part.
preset.comp.3.name: Peak Catcher
preset.comp.3.what: 20:1 with a 0.1 ms attack: about as close to a ceiling as a compressor gets. Not a true limiter - there is no lookahead, so the very first edge of a peak still gets through. Listen for the life going out of the dynamics.
preset.verb.0.name: Vocal Ambience
preset.verb.0.what: A short plate with 40 ms of pre-delay. The gap before the tail starts is what keeps the voice in front of the reverb instead of inside it.
preset.verb.1.name: Concert Hall
preset.verb.1.what: Long decay, large size, wide. Notice how much of the sense of space comes from the size rather than the decay time alone.
preset.verb.2.name: Small Room
preset.verb.2.what: Under a second of decay and higher damping - it reads as a room rather than as an effect. Small rooms are mostly early reflections, which is why this still sounds close.
preset.verb.3.name: Spring Tank
preset.verb.3.what: The metallic, springy character you know from guitar amps. Every repeat round the coil arrives as a chirp - high frequencies travel along a spring faster than low ones - which is why it colours the sound rather than placing it.

verb.desc.room: A small hard room. A short tail, and the first reflections still heard one by one.
verb.desc.hall: A big space. A long, dense tail that arrives late and stays.
verb.desc.plate: A metal sheet, not a room: dense and bright from the first moment, no early reflections.
verb.desc.spring: A spring in a box: a metallic drip and boing, the sound of guitar amps and dub.

eq.general.title: Where things live
eq.general.foot: Choose an instrument above for its own map and a lesson.
eq.lesson.kick.title: Make the kick sit under the bass
eq.lesson.kick.1: Clean the rumble below the kick: high-pass at about 30 Hz.
eq.lesson.kick.2: Find the body - 50-80 Hz - and give it about +3 dB.
eq.lesson.kick.3: Sweep a narrow cut through 200-450 Hz until the cardboard goes away.
eq.lesson.kick.4: Bring out the click at 2-5 kHz so it cuts through the bass.
eq.lesson.snare.title: A snare that cracks instead of ringing
eq.lesson.snare.1: High-pass around 80 Hz: the kick lives below, not the snare.
eq.lesson.snare.2: Give the body a little at 150-250 Hz.
eq.lesson.snare.3: Find the ring between 400 and 900 Hz with a narrow boost, then turn it into a cut.
eq.lesson.bass.title: A bass you can hear on small speakers
eq.lesson.bass.1: High-pass at 30-40 Hz: below that is energy nobody hears.
eq.lesson.bass.2: Cut the mud at 200-400 Hz, where bass and guitars pile up.
eq.lesson.bass.3: Boost the definition at 700 Hz-2 kHz: it is how a phone speaker hears a bass.
eq.lesson.vocal.title: A voice in front of the mix
eq.lesson.vocal.1: High-pass at 80-100 Hz: handling noise and breath rumble, not voice.
eq.lesson.vocal.2: A wide cut in the mud at 150-350 Hz.
eq.lesson.vocal.3: A little presence at 2.5-5 kHz brings the words forward.
eq.lesson.vocal.4: If the esses get sharp, a small narrow cut at 5-9 kHz.
eq.lesson.acoustic.title: An acoustic that does not boom
eq.lesson.acoustic.1: High-pass at about 100 Hz: the body resonance booms close to the mic.
eq.lesson.acoustic.3: A high shelf or bell at 5-12 kHz for the strings' sparkle.
eq.lesson.piano.title: A piano that stays clear in a band
eq.lesson.piano.1: High-pass at 40-60 Hz to leave the bottom to the bass.
eq.lesson.piano.3: Lift the clarity at 2-5 kHz so the chords read.

guide.eq.type.0: Raises or lowers a band around the frequency; Q sets how wide.
guide.eq.type.1: Raises or lowers everything below the frequency, evenly.
guide.eq.type.2: Raises or lowers everything above the frequency, evenly.
guide.eq.type.3: Removes everything below the frequency and lets the highs pass. The first move on most tracks: rumble and handling noise go.
guide.eq.type.4: Removes everything above the frequency and lets the lows pass.
guide.eq.type.5: A very narrow, deep cut - for one ringing resonance or a hum.

guide.eq.slope: Slope: how fast the filter cuts beyond its frequency. 12 dB/oct is gentle, 48 is a wall. Wheel or pinch over the node changes it.
ui.sounds.selectHint: Drag across the waveform to cut your own loop
ui.sounds.trackHint: Select a stretch and save it: on a steady tempo it snaps to whole bars
ui.sounds.fragmentFree: {{seconds}} s, no steady tempo - ends at quiet points
ui.sounds.fragmentTooShort: Too short to be a loop: select at least half a second
live.linkServerError: The server answered with an error ({{code}})
live.linkAppTooOld: This version is too old for Live
live.hintNoNetwork:
Turn on Wi-Fi or plug in a cable.
A local seminar needs no internet - only Wi-Fi shared with the phones.
live.hintNoInternet:
Open any website: if it does not load, the problem is the network, not abcTrain.
Public Wi-Fi (cafe, university) may want a sign-in page first.
A VPN or proxy can get in the way - try without it.
To run a seminar right now, choose Local.
live.hintServerDown:
The internet works, but soundkorb.ru does not answer - probably maintenance; try again in a few minutes.
If soundkorb.ru does not open in a browser either, the fault is on our side.
A work or school network may block it - try another network or mobile data.
To run a seminar right now, choose Local.
live.hintAppTooOld:
Update abcTrain: Settings - About - Check for updates.
Training and local seminars keep working in this version.
live.lanNone: This computer is not on a local network
live.lanNoneHint:
Connect to the venue’s Wi-Fi.
No Wi-Fi? Share a hotspot from this laptop (macOS: Settings - General - Sharing - Internet Sharing; Windows: Settings - Mobile hotspot) and connect the phones to it.
live.lanLinkLocal: The address starts with 169.254: the network has no router, phones will probably not reach it. Use a router or a hotspot.
live.lanTrouble: Phones cannot open the address? Guest Wi-Fi often keeps devices apart - use a normal network or a hotspot. Allow abcTrain incoming connections in the firewall. Turn off mobile data on the phones.
